claims.text: Selectively removing one or more elements from equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni diminishes local lattice distortion in its single-phase FCC quaternary and ternary subsets.
Changes in local lattice distortion alter the effective stacking-fault energy.
Effective stacking-fault energy modulates dislocation mobility and the balance between slip and deformation twinning.
The balance between dislocation slip and deformation twinning governs variations in yield strength and ductility among these alloys.
The equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy and the investigated quaternary and ternary subsets can all be prepared as single-phase FCC materials by identical thermomechanical processing.
Reduced compositional complexity decreases local lattice distortion.
Decreased lattice distortion lowers barriers to dislocation motion.
Lower barriers to dislocation motion change the balance between dislocation slip and deformation twinning.
The proposed change in deformation mechanism produces lower yield strength in the quaternary and ternary alloys than in the equiatomic quinary baseline.
The proposed change in deformation mechanism alters ductility relative to the equiatomic quinary baseline.
Quaternary and ternary subsets will exhibit less local lattice distortion than equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni.
Reduced lattice distortion in the subsets will be evidenced by narrower XRD peak broadening and changes in pair-distribution-function metrics.
The extent of lattice distortion and effective stacking-fault energy will correlate systematically with mechanical properties.
The proposed relationship is limited to single-phase FCC alloys in which processing defects, secondary phases, and major microstructural heterogeneities do not dominate mechanical response.
The hypothesis may fail in phase-separated systems or when strengthening mechanisms other than the proposed lattice-distortion pathway predominate.
The contribution of stacking-fault-energy changes to the slip-twinning balance may vary with temperature and deformation rate.
TEM observations of dislocation structures and twins can distinguish changes in the active deformation mechanisms.
